definition: Jubilant means overflowing with triumphant joy — happiness that celebrates out loud, usually over a victory or a long-awaited success.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word jubilant. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know jubilant should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: When the inspectors finally cleared the dam, the jubilant town rang the firehouse bell until well past midnight.
Glad is far milder than jubilant: gladness is a warm inner yes that may never reach the face, while jubilant joy is louder and fuller — it cheers, it celebrates, it draws a crowd.

Ecstatic is stronger than jubilant: a jubilant crowd is still celebrating a win it can name, while ecstasy is joy so intense and overwhelming that the moment itself dissolves — beyond celebrating, beyond words.

Triumphant centers on the victory itself — the winner's stance over a beaten challenge; a team can be triumphant in grim silence. Jubilant centers on the joy: noisy, overflowing celebration of whatever has been won.

Overjoyed says the happiness has exceeded its container — but it can stay private, a hand pressed over the mouth. Jubilant joy goes public: it cheers, rings bells, and pulls a crowd into the celebrating.

Jubilee came from Hebrew yobel — the ram's-horn trumpet that proclaimed a festival year of freed slaves and forgiven debts. Passing through Latin on its way to English, it bumped into jubilare, and the two have been mistaken for family ever since: the horn lent the shout its occasion, and the shout lent the horn its spelling.
Jubilant means overflowing with triumphant joy — happiness that celebrates out loud, usually over a victory or a long-awaited success.
When the final buzzer confirmed the upset, the jubilant bench emptied — players piling into a heap at center court, seniors hugging the equipment manager, somebody spraying water like champagne.
Jubilant joy is triumphant and loud: it follows a win, and it must celebrate.
Notice there is nothing quiet in the scene — piling, hugging, spraying — because jubilation without an outlet stops being jubilation.
That victorious, out-loud quality is what separates it from mere happiness.
Jubilant is victory's adjective: it wants a scoreboard, a verdict, a reopened road — some named success to celebrate.
Its unit-mates split the neighborhood: elated is the altitude of the feeling, exult is the act of letting it out, and ebullient bubbles by temperament, win or no win.
If nothing has been won, jubilant is the wrong word — and if the joy is silent, it isn't jubilant yet.

For six years the Orpheum's marquee said only CLOSED, and Miller Street learned to walk past without looking up.
The reopening was announced for a Friday.
By noon the sidewalk was full; by dusk the crowd stretched past the hardware store.
When the marquee lights finally stuttered on, the street went jubilant: whistles, hats in the air, a conga line that swallowed the ticket queue.
The projectionist, eighty-one and back at his old post, said the noise reached him through two closed doors, and that he had waited six years to hear exactly that.
Nobody remembers which film ran first.
The celebration outside was the show.
